Signal Basics

Use this interactive during our class discussion to practice account setup, connecting with a friend, choosing privacy settings, and responding to suspicious requests. Make a choice, review the feedback, and try again when needed. The goal is to build habits you can use in everyday conversations.

Practice only. Nothing is sent. No installation, sign-in, permissions, or account details are needed. All practice and progress stay in this page’s memory. Reloading or Reset Exploration clears them, including the certificate.

A friend asks you to move a conversation to Signal. What changes, and what do you still need to check?

Signal uses an internet connection for private messages, voice messages, photos, files, and voice or video calls between Signal users. It does not send ordinary carrier text messages: SMS (Short Message Service) carries text, and MMS (Multimedia Messaging Service) carries pictures and other media. Both participants need Signal.

Purpose and benefits of secure messaging

Secure messaging helps protect the contents of conversations as messages and calls travel between participants’ devices. Everyday information deserves privacy, even when it is not a secret.

  • Keep personal conversations private. Family updates, appointments, photos, and travel plans can stay between the people involved, rather than being readable by the messaging service or someone intercepting the connection.
  • Choose how you communicate. Signal protects text messages, shared photos and files, voice messages, and voice or video calls between Signal users.
  • Control how people contact you. Phone-number privacy settings and usernames let you make choices about how new contacts find you and what information they see. You will practice those choices here.

What do we mean when we say a message is secure?

A secure messaging app helps keep a message private, protects it from being secretly changed on the way, and gives you a way to check that you’re connected to the person you meant to contact.

For example, if you send a friend a door code, you want only your friend to be able to read it and to receive the same code you sent. You also want to know you opened the right conversation before you send it.

End-to-end encryption scrambles message and call contents so only the participants’ devices can read or hear them. Signal cannot read those messages or listen to those calls. You still need to check who is on the other end and decide what to share.

  • A recipient can copy a message or photograph the screen.
  • Someone who can see an unlocked screen can read what is on it.
  • A familiar name or photo does not prove identity.
  • Urgent demands for money, codes, or secrecy are reasons to pause and verify independently.

How do I know if a Signal message is really secure?

Signal-to-Signal messages and calls use end-to-end encryption automatically. You do not need to turn on a separate secure mode. To check the conversation before sharing something sensitive:

  1. Use the real app. Install Signal from its official download page or your device’s official app store, keep it updated, and communicate with another Signal user.
  2. Check the connection with someone you know. A safety number is a code for checking the security of a one-to-one chat—a conversation between two people. In an accepted conversation, open the chat’s settings by selecting the contact’s name at the top, then choose View Safety Number. Compare the number with your contact in person or by calling a number you already know belongs to them.
  3. Pause if the safety number changes unexpectedly. A new phone or reinstallation can cause a change. Confirm with your contact before sending sensitive information.

A matching safety number checks the connection; it does not establish someone’s real-world identity. Encryption also cannot stop a recipient from copying a message or someone from reading an unlocked screen. Check the person, the request, and the security of your device as well as the messaging app.

Signal’s explanation of message privacy · How to check a safety number

Can’t Apple or Google see my messages?

Not through Signal’s normal encrypted delivery. Using Signal on an iPhone or Android phone does not, by itself, give Apple or Google readable copies of the messages traveling between Signal users.

Your phone is a separate part of the privacy picture. Its operating system is the software that runs the device. A message must be decrypted—made readable—on your device for you to read it. A compromised phone, or another app or assistant allowed to read the screen, can expose that readable content.

  • Review assistant access. An AI assistant is software such as Siri or Gemini that can answer questions or act on information. Signal documents screen protections against these assistants on supported versions. Check the settings and guidance for your device rather than assuming every version behaves the same way.
  • Limit notification previews. A notification preview shows part of a message in an alert, sometimes on a locked screen. Choose how much Signal’s notifications display.
  • Keep device protection in place. Update Signal and the phone, use a screen lock, and be careful about giving other software access to your screen. Content you copy into another app or assistant is outside the Signal conversation.

Signal’s screen-security and assistant-access guidance · Signal notification settings and help

Start real installation from Signal’s official download page or your device’s official app store. A permission lets an app use a device feature, such as its microphone or camera. Read each permission prompt; this practice never requests permissions.

Get Connected

Set up an account

Registration means setting up a Signal account. For the phone-number setup covered here, use an existing number that can receive a text or call. Follow Signal’s official registration guidance on your device.

  • A verification code (also called a registration code) is a code Signal sends by text or call to confirm that you control that phone number. Enter it only in the real Signal app’s registration process. Never send it to another person.
  • Your profile is the name and optional photo other people see in Signal. A profile display name is the name you choose for that profile; different people can use the same name.
  • A Signal PIN (personal identification number) is a private code you choose, using numbers or a mix of letters and numbers. It helps recover your profile, settings, and contacts if you switch devices. It is different from the verification code and your phone’s unlock code. It does not restore chat messages.

Connect without exchanging phone numbers

An optional username is a unique name made from letters, numbers, and optionally underscores that someone can use to start a Signal chat with you. It is different from your profile display name. Signal has no public username directory—a searchable list of people’s usernames.

You can share the exact username, its link (a web address that opens a way to contact you), or its QR code (a square barcode someone scans with a camera). Use a trusted channel: a way you already know reaches the right person, such as speaking in person or calling a number you already have.

A message request is an invitation to start a conversation. The recipient—the person receiving it—can accept it or decline it. A username or familiar display name alone does not prove who someone is.

Practice Privacy Settings

This is a concept simulator for a number-based account, not a literal device screen. Official guidance uses the labels below; layout may vary by device and version. No real settings change.

A default is a setting’s starting choice. Visibility means who can see your phone number in Signal. Discovery means who can look up your number to start a Signal chat. These are separate choices.

Disappearing messages are new messages set to be deleted after a chosen time. The timer is that time limit for this chat; it is not a guarantee that nobody can save a copy.

Current practice settings

Number-based defaults: visibility Nobody; discovery Everybody. People who saved your number still know it. Discovery Nobody requires visibility Nobody.

Real-World Choices

A safety number is a code for checking the security of a one-to-one Signal conversation—a chat between two people. Comparing it with a contact through a trusted channel checks the connection; you still need to establish who that person is.

Report means flagging a suspicious account to Signal. Block means preventing that account from contacting you through Signal.

A group invitation link is a web address that lets someone request to join a group chat. An admin (administrator) is a member who can manage the group. Admin approval means an administrator must approve a request to join through the link.

Choose a sound response in each fictional case. Feedback explains how to revise a choice; retries are unlimited.

Group Calls & Links

A group call is a live voice or video conversation with several people. Signal encrypts group calls end to end, just as it does messages.

Call people in an existing group chat

  1. Open the group chat in Signal and select the video camera button.
  2. Choose Start Call to begin, or Join Call if the call is already underway.
  3. During the call, you can mute your microphone, turn your camera off, or raise your hand to let others know you’d like to speak.

Invite people to a call with a link

A call link is a web address that opens an invitation to a call. People who already use Signal can join from the link without joining a group chat. A group invitation link invites someone to join the ongoing group chat.

To make a call link, open Calls in Signal and choose Create a Call Link. You can require approval before people join. Share the link with the people you intend to invite.

What if someone hasn’t installed Signal?

They can open the link in a web browser, but they can’t join the call there. To join, they need to install Signal from an official source, set up their account, and reopen the link in Signal. If the organizer requires approval, they’ll need to wait to be admitted. If they prefer to skip installation, agree on another way to talk.
